ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Jack London

code.originalText: Establishing care for tiredness and ankle swelling, with high blood pressure and abnormal kidney tests, and heavy drinking found at the visit: kidney, liver and alcohol tests, AUDIT and DSM-5-TR assessment, withdrawal planning, mood and safety, his writing schedule, and a nephrology consultation

text.paragraph: Establishing care for tiredness and ankle swelling, with high blood pressure and abnormal kidney tests, and heavy drinking found at the visit: kidney, liver and alcohol tests, AUDIT and DSM-5-TR assessment, withdrawal planning, mood and safety, his writing schedule, and a nephrology consultation [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Tired by afternoon, with swollen ankles, and frightened by the word 'kidneys' again. [S]
He knows the drinking is hurting him and wants to stop without losing his work. [S]
He wants to keep writing a thousand words every morning. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: He was born on January 12, 1876, in San Francisco, and his birth certificate named him John Griffith Chaney. His mother, Flora Wellman, had lived with William Chaney, an astrologer, who left before the birth; she married John London, who adopted and raised the boy. [D]
He grew up poor and worked from boyhood: an oyster pirate at 15, on the fish patrol at 16, an able-bodied seaman at 17, and a tramp crossing America at 18, when he spent a month in jail. [D]
He went to the Klondike gold fields in 1897, at 21, and came home with very little after suffering scurvy. [D]

He became internationally famous with The Call of the Wild (1903) and The Sea Wolf (1904), completed more than 50 books between 1900 and 1916, was at his peak the highest paid writer in the United States, and pushed to write 1,000 words a day wherever he was. [D]

From 1905 he bought land at Glen Ellen in the Sonoma Valley and built up his Beauty Ranch; Wolf House, his nearly finished stone and redwood home, burned on August 22, 1913, a crushing financial loss. The loss left him depressed, but he forced himself back to work. [D]

On the voyage of his yacht Snark through the South Pacific (1907 to 1909), in the Solomon Islands he had sores that a physician in Fiji called yaws and a missionary said were not; his hands swelled and peeled and his toenails thickened, a malady the Australian specialists could not name; he spent five weeks in hospital in Australia, gave up the voyage, and blamed tropical light. He also had a 'silvery skin' that doctors called by old names for leprosy, which cleared without treatment in California. [D]

Physicians writing since have interpreted his illnesses differently: the 'silvery skin' has been read as psoriasis; one review proposed that mercury used to treat yaws damaged his kidneys and caused a dermatitis of the hands, feet and face; others suggested lupus, gout, and the effects of tobacco, alcohol and diet on his blood pressure and kidneys. None is established. [R]

In John Barleycorn (1913) he wrote of his drinking from the first time he got drunk, at five years old. He held that he was no born alcoholic and had acquired the taste, and described how at the ranch, after writing his thousand words between nine and eleven each morning, he began to take a cocktail before midday dinner and then alone, 'not for the sake of the taste, but for the effect of the drink.' [D]
In July 1913 he had his appendix removed, and serious kidney damage was found; his physician diagnosed a significant kidney problem at that time. [D]
In 1914 he went to Vera Cruz as a war correspondent in the Mexican Revolution and was ill with dysentery and rheumatism. [D]
He spent February 24 to July 22, 1915, in Hawaii and sailed there again on December 16, 1915; his health was described that year as declining. [D]
He married Bess Maddern in 1900; their daughters Joan and Bess were born in 1901 and 1902, and the marriage ended in divorce in 1905. He married Charmian Kittredge in November 1905. [D]

Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: Novelist and journalist, internationally known; writes a thousand words every morning from nine to eleven, six or seven days a week, under steady pressure to pay for the ranch and to help others; farms and breeds livestock on a large ranch in the Sonoma Valley [S]
Married; two daughters from an earlier marriage; lives on the ranch; back two weeks from five months in Hawaii [S]

Drinks whisky most days: the first drink when the morning's writing is done, more through the afternoon and evening, a bottle or more on most days for years, and a drink on waking some mornings to steady his hands; has tried to cut down on his own several times; AUDIT 27 [S]
Smokes about ten cigarettes a day; no other substances; no opioids or sleeping pills [S]
Eats one large meal a day, often rare meat, with little fruit or vegetables; heavy salt; rides and swims in the afternoons when he is well [S]
Keeps a rifle and a shotgun on the ranch for livestock and hunting [S]
Strengths: an iron habit of daily work, curiosity and humor, his love of the ranch and the sea, a frank and detailed understanding of his own drinking, and his own decision to come in now [S]

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, warm and quick; speech fluent, at times emphatic; mood 'worn down'; affect full; slight tremor of the outstretched hands; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; insight good and judgment fair; PHQ-9 9 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 7. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

code.displayName: Physical findings of General status Narrative

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent; still writes every morning but tires by afternoon; rides less than he did; knee and low back pain after riding. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-08-04; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Alert, warm and quick; speech fluent, at times emphatic; mood 'worn down'; affect full; slight tremor of the outstretched hands; no psychotic symptoms; no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; insight good and judgment fair; PHQ-9 9 with item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 7. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: severe alcohol use disorder, a new chronic illness, financial pressure, mild depressive and anxiety symptoms, and firearms on the ranch. He agreed that the rifle and shotgun will be kept locked in the ranch office safe with the ammunition stored apart, and that he will not handle them after drinking. Chlordiazepoxide is dispensed for five days only, with a daily telephone check. A written safety plan was made with him, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) and the clinic's number were written on a card he carries. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to the documented kidney damage found in 1913; superseded when the consultation staged chronic kidney disease.

Alcohol use disorder, severe (seven DSM-5-TR criteria): a bottle of whisky or more most days for years, a morning drink to steady his hands, failed attempts to cut down, and drinking despite knowing it harms his health; AUDIT 27; PEth 410 ng/mL
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his own published account of heavy drinking; the criteria, scores and amounts are synthetic and are not a claim about his real drinking.
Daily self-directed naproxen for knee and back pain for about two years, stopped at intake; acetaminophen in its place
S — Synthetic medication history; the joint pain is anchored to the documented rheumatism of 1914, which is not given a diagnosis.

list.item: Tiredness, ankle swelling and high blood pressure (158/98 mmHg) with a raised creatinine (1.98 mg/dL, eGFR 43) and albumin in the urine (240 mg/g), found at intake; a creatinine of 1.7 mg/dL at an insurance examination about fourteen months ago, by his account; chronicity and cause under evaluation with a nephrology consultation: active, confirmed [S]

Alcohol use disorder, severe (seven DSM-5-TR criteria): a bottle of whisky or more most days for years, a morning drink to steady his hands, failed attempts to cut down, and drinking despite knowing it harms his health; AUDIT 27; PEth 410 ng/mL: active, confirmed [S]
Daily self-directed naproxen for knee and back pain for about two years, stopped at intake; acetaminophen in its place: active, confirmed [S]
Cigarette smoking, about ten a day; not ready to stop while he stops drinking: active, confirmed [S]

Kidneys and blood pressure: creatinine with eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021), urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and urinalysis with microscopy, electrolytes and bicarbonate, uric acid, calcium, phosphate and PTH, blood count, HbA1c and a lipid panel once; the earlier insurance creatinine obtained; ultrasound of the kidneys and liver; standardized office blood pressure at every visit and home readings. Guideline: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease (2024); KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease (2021); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease, hypertension and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Nephrology consultation to confirm the stage and cause of the kidney disease and advise on blood pressure, an SGLT2 inhibitor, medicines for alcohol use disorder at his kidney function, and pain relief. Guideline: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease (2024); KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease (2021) [S]

Losartan 50 mg daily from intake, raised to the maximum tolerated dose, with potassium and creatinine two to four weeks after each start or change, accepting a rise in creatinine of up to 30 percent; less salt. Guideline: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease (2021); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease, hypertension and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Alcohol: AUDIT, DSM-5-TR criteria and PEth with consent; liver tests and FIB-4; a withdrawal-risk score (PAWSS) and outpatient withdrawal with a five-day chlordiazepoxide taper, daily telephone checks and thiamine; addiction-focused counseling with the clinic's addiction medicine team each week and mutual-help meetings if he wishes; PEth and liver tests at follow-up. Guideline: The American Psychiatric Association Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder (2018); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Substance Use Disorders (2021); The ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020); AASLD Practice Guideline on blood-based noninvasive liver disease assessment of hepatic fibrosis and steatosis (2025) [S]

Pain and medicine safety: no naproxen, ibuprofen or other oral anti-inflammatory medicines; acetaminophen up to 2,000 mg a day; no opioids or tramadol with kidney disease and in early recovery, and none at all if naltrexone is started; any new medicine checked for kidney dosing. Guideline: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, chronic kidney disease, hypertension and depression monographs (2026) [S]

Safety: a structured safety assessment, firearms locked with ammunition apart, small supplies of withdrawal medicine, a written safety plan, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Work and recovery: keep the morning writing hours from nine to eleven; replace the late-morning drink with a swim or a ride; no alcohol kept in the writing room; PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and follow-up. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Substance Use Disorders (2021); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]
Tobacco: advice to stop, with nicotine replacement or varenicline offered when he is ready. Guideline: Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]
Referral to nephrology, Teodor Mbatha-Rasmussen, MD, ordered 2026-08-04 [S]
